title: Literary Devices
description: Common literary devices with plain definitions and short examples, for English class, essay writing, and close reading.
subject: arts-humanities

cards.definition: Describes one thing as if it were another, without using "like" or "as." Example: "The hallway was a river of backpacks."
The audience knows something that a character does not, creating tension or humor.
Hints early in a story about events that will happen later.
Compares two unlike things using "like" or "as." Example: "The puppy was as restless as a spinning top."
Gives human qualities to something non-human. Example: "The old car groaned up the hill."
Repeats the same starting consonant sound in nearby words. Example: "Seven sleepy sailors sang softly."
Repeats vowel sounds in nearby words. Example: "Rain made the lane gray."
A word that imitates the sound it names, such as buzz, crash, or sizzle.
Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect. Example: "This backpack weighs a ton."
Presents something as less important than it really is. Example: calling a hurricane "a bit of wind."
Saying the opposite of what you mean. Example: "What lovely weather," said during a downpour.
An outcome turns out to be the opposite of what was expected. Example: a fire station burns down.
Two contradictory words placed side by side. Example: "a deafening silence."
A statement that seems to contradict itself but reveals a deeper truth. Example: "The more I learn, the less I know."
Vivid sensory language that helps the reader see, hear, smell, taste, or feel a scene.
Using an object, character, or event to stand for a larger idea, such as a dove representing peace.
A recurring image, object, or idea in a work that helps develop its theme.
A brief reference to a well-known person, place, event, or work. Example: calling a huge job "a Herculean task."
Placing contrasting elements side by side to highlight their differences.
Repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses. Example: "Every day I wait. Every day I wonder."
A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh or blunt one. Example: "passed away" instead of "died."
A scene that interrupts the present action to show events from the past.
The perspective a story is told from, such as first person ("I") or third person ("she," "they").
